description: Expected §10 error codes for unresolvable symbols, malformed strings, out-of-range exponents, and unsupported grammar versions.

cases.rationale: Well-formed under the grammar, absent from the registry. §6.3 is explicit that strict mode MUST reject unresolvable symbols.

The parser raises the same code in both modes; mode selects what the READER does with it, not whether parsing fails. That layering matters because §8.4 says working tables have no mode at all, so a mode-dependent parser would have undefined behavior on the most common artifact. AMB-021 recommends the permissive reader catch this, warn once, taint the column, and preserve the original string verbatim for round-trip.
Two operators in a row. §10 has no code for a parse failure — E_UNKNOWN_UNIT is about symbol resolution, and reporting "unknown unit MW**h" would send the user to check their registry over a typo.
Trailing operator with no right-hand term.
§6.1 states there are no parentheses. Their absence is what makes left-to-right division binding unambiguous, so accepting them would quietly reintroduce the grouping question.

Two symbols separated only by whitespace. This case replaced `MW * h` when AMB-006 was revised: spaces at the edges and around operators are now accepted, because they cannot change meaning, but a space between symbols can. Collapsing `m s` to `ms` yields millisecond — a different dimension, silently — and reading the space as multiplication would give the product a second spelling. The error names the fix instead of guessing.

§6.1 calls out this exact string as invalid — numeric prefixes and scale factors are not allowed inside unit strings; prefixed units are distinct registry entries. The spec says invalid but names no code, which is the only reason this case is provisional.

°C is degC's display.unicode form, not a symbol. Display forms are output-only. Under AMB-005's ASCII symbol class the degree sign cannot begin a symbol, so this is a syntax error rather than an unknown unit — a distinction that only exists once the lexical class is actually defined.
An explicit plus sign is a second spelling of ^2. Rejecting keeps one spelling per expression; accepting would require step 3 to normalize it, which §6.3 does not mention.
§6.2 fixes dimension exponents at signed 8-bit; §6.1 puts no bound on unit-string exponents. 200 is grammatically valid and dimensionally unrepresentable, and §10 has no code for the gap.

Each term is individually in range; the merge overflows. The range check therefore belongs after §6.3 step 2, not in the lexer — an implementation that only validates per-term silently wraps to -56 here.

The wire declares a grammar newer than this implementation supports. The unit string itself is perfectly valid under grammar 1 — the failure is the version claim, and guessing would be how a v2 rational exponent gets silently misread.

Rational exponents are excluded from grammar v1 and deferred to v2 (§12). Under v1 this lexes as m^1 divided by the term "2", and 2 is not a symbol. A v1 implementation must not partially honour v2 syntax.
